extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists; students of fiction and creative-writing practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on composing a novel: selecting its dominant type and mode of presentation, controlling scale, point of view, characters, dialogue, descriptive passage, and methods for conveying the passage of time and verisimilitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of explicit/objectionable material
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the reactionary 'now-that-it-can-be-told' school and 'dirt-for-dirt's-sake'; explicitness alone does not make art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit or sensational material should not be used merely for shock; the novelist must 'see life steadily' rather than 'recount it whole.' Historical examples: Butler's sober handling of difficult subjects vs. contemporary pornography mistaken for genius. The balance will right itself as novelists learn restraint and the public becomes more thoughtful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of novel type (manners, character/psychology, adventure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most novels may be grouped as novels of manners, of character (psychology), or of adventure; this choice defines the method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classifying a subject determines the manner and angle of vision (examples: 'Vanity Fair' for manners, 'Madame Bovary' for character, 'Rob Roy' for adventure). Subdivisions and hybrids (farcical manners, romance, philosophical romance) exist; the author must decide which method to use because the same subject can be treated in very different ways depending on the chosen manner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode of presentation determined by subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode of presenting the material (narrative, dialogue, play-like treatment) must be determined by the nature of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative, with its flexibility, generally furnishes the substance of the novel and permits passing from one form of presentation to another; dialogue and theatrical artifices are appropriate only when the subject demands them. Avoid adding the 'shackles of another form' unless required by the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use dialogue sparingly and purposefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Dialogue should be an adjunct to narrative, reserved for culminating moments and used as a flavouring, not the main vehicle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive dialogue creates presentness but wastes space and forces characters to state the obvious, producing diluted 'by-talk' and improbability (Trollope's rambling conversations as an anti-pattern). Dialogue breaks into short paragraphs and enhances climaxes when used sparingly; overuse tires the reader and makes later chapters feel paid-for. Example of misapplied dialogue: Henry James's experiment in writing largely in dialogue ('The Awkward Age') which arguably loses central problems in talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scale: short story vs novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose scale according to the subject: short stories are improvisations suited to foreshortened dramatic climaxes; novels require space for gradual unfolding and analysis over intervals of time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novel often needs to mark the lapse of time and permit minute analysis of successive states of feeling; even a story about one person over a few hours can be a novel if the subject's character requires it. Do not force a novel's subject into a short-story form if it would lose significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain or achieve objective creative distance (autobiography vs novel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Autobiographical/subjective tales often lack the objective faculty necessary for novelistic invention; the novelist should be able to view the story as a whole rather than as mere self-analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Autobiographical novels are often fragments of autobiography rather than true novels, because minor characters become satellites of the central self. Exceptions exist when the author achieves 'magic transposition' so the material becomes an objective creation (e.g., Tolstoy's 'The Kreutzer Sonata' being as objective as Othello). A novelist should strive to transpose personal material into an objectively creative form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unnecessary double/parallel plots; ensure organic interweaving
rubrics_metrics.description: The Victorian 'double plot' (two parallel series of adventures alternating without deep connection) is a tedious convention; modern novels should avoid this unless the groups are organically interwoven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The double-plot trick differs from genuinely interwoven social panoramas (Thackeray, Balzac). Young writers are tempted to crowd scenes with supernumeraries; instead choose principal characters so typical they can connote whole sections of social background and reduce the need for parallel story-lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and relevance of characters and scenic detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Only include characters and scenic details that are necessary and relevant to the projected tale; relevance is the first necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters and props should serve the action: don't create characters without first following them to the projected end. Theatre rules (objects on stage must be necessary) are useful guides: fewer, well-studied characters and details often produce a deeper effect than multiplying half-drawn figures. Examples: George Meredith making landscape contribute to interpretation; avoid irrelevant supernumeraries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive passages must be filtered through a character's perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions (landscape, street, house) should be depicted only insofar as they would be noticed by the intelligence concerned and in that intelligence's register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the impression of places an event in the history of a soul. Anti-pattern: detailed geological/agricultural descriptions that the character would not notice (Hardy's detailed Wessex vale as a negative example). Positive example: evocative settings that reflect a character's inner life (Egdon Heath as Eustacia Vye sees it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control point of view: limit shifting and choose reflecting consciousnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide from which characters the subject is to be seen; work from not more than two (or at most three) angles of vision and shift as seldom as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose reflectors in close mental/moral relation or discerning enough to estimate each other so the tale presents as a whole despite shifts. Only shift when the first reflector cannot plausibly be aware of or react to events; let the subject determine when adjacent consciousnesses must take up the tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain verisimilitude; avoid intrusive omniscience and authorial showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Verisimilitude is 'the truth of art'; avoid slovenly tumbling in and out of characters' minds and sudden authorial scrutiny that breaks the illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial intrusions and implausible contrivances (e.g., characters created solely to eavesdrop and report, like James's Assinghams) undermine reader confidence. Study experiments by James and Conrad: James confined details to an eye fixed on it; Conrad employed a 'hall of mirrors' of reflecting consciousnesses. Balzac's use of fragments reflected in accidental participants ('La Grande Breteche') is a positive model for building verisimilitude without clumsy omniscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey the passage of time through subtle transitional narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate the gradual passage of time so character changes feel like natural growth rather than arbitrary sleight-of-hand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inconspicuous transitional pages of narrative between climaxes; do not fear to go slowly. Keep down the tone of the narrative in intervals—'as colourless and quiet as life often is'—so erosion or accretion of character seems inevitable. Study Balzac, Thackeray and Tolstoy for methods of suggesting development in ordinary narrative transition.
